reigns.tagline: The first Czech duke who steps out of the legends
reigns.previously: Legend: Libuše foresees Prague and weds Přemysl the Ploughman.
paragraphs: Every Czech child knows the legend. The wise princess Libuše had a vision of a great city whose glory would touch the stars, and that became Prague. Her people wanted a man to rule them, so she sent riders to find a ploughman named Přemysl, who left his oxen in the field to marry her. It is a lovely story, first written down by the priest Cosmas around 1120. The real history starts with Bořivoj, the first Přemyslid we can actually pin down.

In his day Bohemia was a patchwork of tribes in the shadow of Great Moravia, a powerful Slav state to the east. Bořivoj was one of several Czech dukes, and he did well by staying close to the Moravian ruler Svatopluk. The later legends say he was baptised at Svatopluk's court by Methodius, the missionary who brought the Slavs their own church language. Back home he built little churches at Levý Hradec and on the hill that became Prague Castle.

His wife Ludmila became a Christian with him and outlived him by decades. Bořivoj died young, around 889, leaving two boys. They were too small to rule, and for a few years Svatopluk of Moravia called the shots in Bohemia.

claims.text: Bořivoj was the 'Goriwei' named among Czech dukes beaten by the Franks in 872.
claims.note: The Annals of Fulda list a Goriwei that year. The names look alike, but nothing else ties the two together.

claims.text: Methodius himself baptised Bořivoj at the Moravian court.
claims.note: Told by the Legend of Christian (late 10th century) and by Cosmas. No source from Bořivoj's own time mentions it.

claims.text: Libuše and Přemysl the Ploughman founded the dynasty.
claims.note: Known only from Cosmas, writing over two centuries after Bořivoj. Nobody can show they existed.

reigns.hook: Bořivoj is gone and his sons are boys. When the elder, Spytihněv, comes of age, Great Moravia is cracking, and he must decide which way Bohemia will bow.

reigns.tagline: The duke who turned Bohemia to face the West
reigns.previously: Bořivoj dies young. Moravia's Svatopluk runs Bohemia for a while.
paragraphs: Spytihněv was the elder of Bořivoj's two boys, and the first Přemyslid to rule in his own right. Some lists start his reign in 889, straight after his father, but for those first years the real boss was Svatopluk of Great Moravia. Then in 894 Svatopluk died, his sons began fighting each other, and the Czech dukes saw a way out.

In the summer of 895 Spytihněv and another duke, Vitislav, rode to Regensburg and did homage to Arnulf, king of the East Franks. It was a turning point. From now on Bohemia looked west to the German kings, not east to Moravia. Within about a dozen years Magyar horsemen had wrecked Great Moravia. Bohemia came through.

At home Spytihněv made Prague his base. Strong walls went up around the castle hill, and a ring of forts such as Budeč guarded the heartland. He died in 915, around forty, and left no son we know of. The duchy passed to his younger brother.

claims.text: Spytihněv and Vitislav did homage to King Arnulf at Regensburg in 895.
claims.note: The Annals of Fulda name both men as leaders of the Bohemian dukes that year.

claims.text: He built the first strong ramparts of Prague Castle and the fort at Budeč.
claims.note: Archaeology dates big works at both sites to about his time. Pinning them on him personally is a guess.

claims.text: His reign began in 889, right after his father's death.
claims.note: Some Czech lists say so. Others start it in 894, when Moravian control ended. The sources are too thin to decide.

reigns.hook: Spytihněv is dead without an heir. His younger brother Vratislaus takes Prague, and his bride from the far north will soon split the family.

reigns.tagline: Father of a saint, husband of a feared duchess
reigns.previously: Spytihněv I dies in 915. His younger brother is next.
paragraphs: Vratislaus (Vratislav in Czech) took over in 915. Years earlier he had married Drahomíra, a princess from the Slav tribes on the Havel river, far to the north. She gave him at least two sons who would shape Czech history: Wenceslaus and Boleslaus. Vratislaus's mother, the pious Ludmila, was still alive and very much part of the household.

His short reign was a dangerous time. Great Moravia was gone, and the Magyars raided far and wide across central Europe. Tradition says Vratislaus founded the basilica of St George at Prague Castle, which became the family's burial church. It still stands on the castle hill, rebuilt many times since.
On 13 February 921 he died, still in his early thirties. Wenceslaus was only a boy of about thirteen, and Bohemia needed a regent. Ludmila and Drahomíra both wanted the job.

claims.text: Drahomíra was a pagan princess of the Hevelli.
claims.note: The saints' legends make her a Hevellian and hostile to the Church. Her origin is likely; her paganism may be later spin.

claims.text: Vratislaus founded St George's Basilica at Prague Castle.
claims.note: Tradition and Cosmas credit him. Archaeology shows an early church there, but who started it isn't certain.

claims.text: He was killed fighting the Magyars.
claims.note: Some historians link his early death to a Magyar raid around 921. No early source says how he died.

reigns.hook: The duke is dead and his heir is a child. Grandmother Ludmila raises the boy as a Christian. His mother Drahomíra has other ideas.

reigns.tagline: The good duke murdered by his own brother
reigns.previously: Vratislaus dies in 921. His son Wenceslaus is still a child.
paragraphs: Wenceslaus (Václav) was a boy when his father died, and the women around him went to war. His grandmother Ludmila had raised him as a Christian. His mother Drahomíra wanted control. In September 921 men sent by Drahomíra killed Ludmila at her castle of Tetín. Ludmila became a saint. A few years later, around 924 or 925, Wenceslaus took power himself and sent his mother away.

He was pious, bookish and builder of a church of St Vitus at Prague Castle. He was also a realist. When the German king Henry the Fowler marched on Prague in 929, Wenceslaus submitted and paid tribute. Some nobles hated that. So did his younger brother Boleslaus. In September 935 Boleslaus invited him to a feast at Stará Boleslav. Next morning, on his way to church, Wenceslaus was cut down at the door.

Within decades he was a saint, and later the patron of the whole Czech land. He was a duke, never a king; the King Wenceslaus I of three centuries later is a different man. The English carol 'Good King Wenceslas' was written by J. M. Neale in 1853 and is pure invention.

claims.text: Ludmila was strangled with her own veil.
claims.note: The detail comes from the saints' lives written decades later. They agree she was strangled; the veil may be pious decoration.

claims.text: Wenceslaus was killed in 935.
claims.note: Most historians accept 935. Some early legends point to 929, and the debate has never quite closed.

claims.text: An army of knights sleeps inside Blaník hill, waiting for Wenceslaus to lead them when the Czechs are in direst need.
claims.note: A folk legend first recorded centuries later. Still a favourite.

reigns.hook: Wenceslaus lies dead at the church door. His killer is now duke, and he is about to pick a fight with the most powerful man in Europe.

reigns.tagline: The brother-killer who built a Czech state
reigns.previously: Wenceslaus is cut down at the church door. His brother is now duke.
paragraphs: Boleslaus (Boleslav) got the throne with blood on his hands, and he ruled hard. Within a year he was fighting Otto I, the new German king, and the war dragged on for fourteen years. In 950 Otto marched into Bohemia, and Boleslaus gave in. After that he played the loyal vassal, and Bohemian troops rode with Otto when he smashed the Magyars at the Lechfeld in 955.

At home he built a real state, with castles, tribute and his own silver coins. Around 965 a Jewish traveller from Spain, Ibrahim ibn Yaqub, called Prague a busy town of stone where merchants came from far and wide to trade, slaves included. The same year Boleslaus married his daughter Dobrawa to Mieszko I of Poland. Mieszko was baptised a year later, and Poland became Christian.
He died in July, in 967 or 972. His son, also Boleslaus, inherited a strong duchy and a family name that needed some polishing.

claims.text: Boleslaus died in 972.
claims.note: Some annals put his death in 967. The later date fits better with what his son did, and most modern work prefers it.

claims.text: He swore to give his newborn son to the Church as penance for killing Wenceslaus.
claims.note: The story is in the Legend of Christian and Cosmas. It may be a tale told to explain a later monk-son, Strachkvas.

claims.text: Ibrahim ibn Yaqub described Prague as a rich trading town built of stone and lime.
claims.note: His account survives in the 11th-century geographer al-Bakri.

reigns.hook: Boleslaus the Cruel is dead. His son wants to be remembered as a good Christian prince. A bishop of his own would be a fine start.

reigns.tagline: A bishop for Prague and a massacre at Libice
reigns.previously: Boleslaus the Cruel dies. His son of the same name takes over.
paragraphs: Boleslaus II earned the name 'the Pious'. In 973 a bishopric was set up in Prague, and its first bishop arrived in 976. The Czechs had their own church at last. His mints at Prague turned out silver pennies, called denars, that traded across Europe. The second bishop was a Czech noble named Adalbert (Vojtěch), from the rich Slavník clan, which ran its own lands from the fortress of Libice.

Adalbert was a saint in the making and a nightmare to work with. He scolded the Czechs for their slave trade and their loose morals, and twice walked out on his see. In 995, while the Slavník brothers were away, the duke's men stormed Libice on 28 September and killed most of the family left inside. Adalbert never came home. He went off to preach to the pagan Prussians, who killed him in 997.
Boleslaus was ill for years and died in February 999, leaving three sons who hated each other.

claims.text: The Slavník family was massacred at Libice on 28 September 995.
claims.note: Told in the lives of Adalbert and by Thietmar and Cosmas. Who gave the order, and how far the duke was involved, is less clear.

claims.text: Adalbert left Prague because the Czechs would not give up their sinful ways.
claims.note: That's the version in his saints' lives. Politics, and his family's clash with the duke, mattered too.

claims.text: Prague's denars were minted in his name.
claims.note: Many hoards of his coins have been found across northern and eastern Europe.

reigns.hook: The pious duke is dead. His eldest son, Boleslaus the Red, is a brute, his two younger brothers are in danger, and the duke of Poland is watching closely.

reigns.tagline: The red duke who maimed his own brother
reigns.previously: Boleslaus the Pious dies, leaving three quarrelling sons.
paragraphs: Boleslaus III, called 'the Red' (Boleslav Ryšavý), was the eldest son and the most frightening. He trusted nobody, least of all his younger brothers. According to the German bishop Thietmar of Merseburg, he had Jaromír castrated so he could never father heirs. Jaromír, Oldřich and their mother Emma fled to Bavaria.

Things went badly abroad as well. Poland's ambitious duke Bolesław the Brave, Boleslaus's own cousin, had taken Kraków from Bohemia around 999. At home the duke turned on the nobles, who decided he had to go. In 1002 they threw him out. He ran first to the German margrave Henry of Schweinfurt, then to Poland, the one place he should never have trusted.

claims.text: Boleslaus III had his brother Jaromír castrated.
claims.note: Thietmar of Merseburg, writing a few years later, says so. He disliked Czech dukes, but nothing contradicts him.

claims.text: Poland took Kraków from Bohemia around 999.
claims.note: The loss is certain. The exact year, 999 or a little earlier, rests on thin evidence.

reigns.hook: The red duke has fled. The Czech nobles need someone new fast, and they look to a little-known prince with Polish ties.

reigns.tagline: A stopgap duke who drank himself to death
reigns.previously: Boleslaus the Red's nobles throw him out of Prague.
paragraphs: Nobody is quite sure who Vladivoj was. Thietmar says he came from Poland, and many historians think he was a son of Mieszko I and the Czech princess Dobrawa, which would make him a grandson of Boleslaus the Cruel. The Czech nobles needed a duke and he was willing.

He went straight to the new German king, Henry II, and received Bohemia from him as a fief. That was a big step: the duchy now belonged to the German kingdom on paper as well as in practice. Vladivoj did not enjoy it for long. He died in January 1003, and Thietmar sneers that drink was what killed him.

claims.text: Vladivoj was a Piast, a son of Mieszko I of Poland and Dobrawa.
claims.note: A common modern guess based on Thietmar's hints. No source spells out his parents.

claims.text: He drank himself to death.
claims.note: Thietmar of Merseburg says he was a hopeless drinker. Thietmar is hostile and gives no other detail.

claims.text: He took Bohemia as a fief from Henry II in 1002.
claims.note: Thietmar describes the grant at Regensburg. It is the first clear case of a Czech duke holding Bohemia as a royal fief.

reigns.hook: Vladivoj is dead. The nobles bring back Jaromír and Oldřich, but the red duke is coming home too, with a Polish army behind him.

reigns.tagline: Back for revenge, then blinded by his cousin
reigns.previously: Vladivoj dies after a few months as duke.
paragraphs: When Vladivoj died, the nobles brought Jaromír and Oldřich home. They lasted a few weeks. Bolesław the Brave of Poland sent troops to put Boleslaus the Red back on the throne, and the brothers fled again. Boleslaus came back angry. He had a list of the nobles who had betrayed him.

Thietmar says he gathered them at Vyšehrad and killed them, cutting down his own son-in-law with his own hands. Czech historians usually count the Vršovci clan among the victims, and they never forgot. That left Boleslaus feared and friendless. His cousin Bolesław invited him to Kraków for talks, then had him seized and blinded. The red duke spent the rest of his life a prisoner in Poland and died there, probably in 1037.

claims.text: Boleslaus killed his own son-in-law at Vyšehrad.
claims.note: Thietmar reports it in detail. He is the only source and loved a gruesome story about Czech dukes.

claims.text: Bolesław the Brave had his cousin blinded.
claims.note: Thietmar and later Czech writers agree on the blinding. The exact date in 1003 is unclear.

reigns.hook: Prague has no duke and no Přemyslid in reach. The man who blinded Boleslaus is already riding in to take Bohemia for himself.

reigns.tagline: Poland's duke tries to swallow Bohemia whole
reigns.previously: Boleslaus the Red is lured to Kraków and blinded.
paragraphs: Bolesław the Brave (Bolesław Chrobry) was Duke of Poland and the son of a Czech princess, so he could say he had Přemyslid blood. In 1003 he moved into Prague and ruled Bohemia himself. Czech lists sometimes count him as Boleslaus IV. For a moment a great Slav realm seemed to be forming, stretching from the Baltic to the Bohemian forest.

The German king Henry II would not allow it. He offered to let Bolesław keep Bohemia as a vassal, as Vladivoj had done. Bolesław refused. So in the late summer of 1004 Henry marched into Bohemia with the exiled Jaromír at his side. Czech lords came over to them as they went, and the Polish garrison abandoned Prague without a pitched battle.

claims.text: Bolesław refused to hold Bohemia as a fief from Henry II.
claims.note: Thietmar records Henry's offer and the refusal. It turned a dispute into open war.

claims.text: The Polish garrison slipped out of Prague at night.
claims.note: Thietmar describes a hasty retreat as the Czechs rose. Details of the night escape vary between accounts.

reigns.hook: The Poles are gone and Henry II has a Přemyslid in hand. The castrated Jaromír will be duke, on a very short German leash.

reigns.tagline: Restored by the Germans, ousted by his brother
reigns.previously: Henry II marches on Prague. The Polish garrison flees.
paragraphs: Jaromír got his throne from the German king, and he never forgot it. In 1004 Henry II installed him in Prague and he became a model vassal. Czech warriors marched beside the Germans in Henry's long wars against Poland. Bolesław the Brave was the enemy of both men, after all.

Loyalty did not make him popular at home. His younger brother Oldřich had his own friends among the nobles, and in the spring of 1012 he struck. Jaromír lost Prague and fled to Germany to ask Henry for help. The king summoned both brothers, then left Oldřich in charge and kept Jaromír in custody. A useful spare duke might come in handy one day.

claims.text: Jaromír and his Czechs fought alongside Henry II against Poland.
claims.note: Thietmar records Czech contingents in Henry's campaigns, starting in 1005.

claims.text: Henry II held Jaromír in custody after 1012.
claims.note: Thietmar says Jaromír was kept under guard in Germany. How long and how strictly is unclear.

reigns.hook: Oldřich now rules in Prague. He will win back Moravia, fall for a girl at a well, and give the Czechs one of their favourite love stories.

reigns.tagline: The duke who married the girl at the well
reigns.previously: Jaromír rules as Henry II's loyal vassal until 1012.
paragraphs: Oldřich (Udalrich in Latin) took Prague in 1012 and kept it for over twenty years. Cosmas gives him a romance every Czech knows. Riding home from a hunt, he saw a peasant girl named Božena washing linen at a village well, fell for her on the spot and made her his wife. Their son Bretislaus would be one of the great Přemyslids.

He also took back Moravia, which Poland had held for years. That doubled the size of his lands. But the German kings wanted obedience, and Oldřich gave them less of it than Jaromír had. In 1033 the emperor Conrad II called him to answer for himself. Oldřich failed to turn up, was condemned, and ended up a prisoner in Bavaria.

claims.text: Oldřich fell for the peasant girl Božena at a well.
claims.note: The scene comes from Cosmas, about a century later. Božena was real, but her humble birth may be romance.

claims.text: Moravia was recovered from Poland in 1019.
claims.note: Some historians argue for 1019, others for about 1029. The sources are too thin to settle it.

claims.text: Conrad II deposed him for not answering a summons.
claims.note: German annals record the summons in 1033 and Oldřich's exile. Why he stayed away is unknown.

reigns.hook: Oldřich is locked up in Bavaria. Conrad II digs out the spare duke he kept in reserve: the maimed brother Jaromír.

reigns.tagline: The maimed brother gets one more turn
reigns.previously: Conrad II deposes Oldřich and locks him up in Bavaria.
paragraphs: Two decades after losing Prague, Jaromír was back. Conrad II needed a Přemyslid he could trust, and the old exile fitted. Oldřich's son Bretislaus was given a share of Moravia. For a moment the family seemed settled.

It did not last. In 1034 Conrad freed Oldřich, and Oldřich came straight home. Jaromír was shoved aside within months. His brother had him blinded and shut away at Lysá on the Elbe. Even there he was not safe. On 4 November 1035 he was murdered, and Cosmas blames the Vršovci, the clan the Přemyslids had already spilled so much blood over.

claims.text: Jaromír and Oldřich briefly shared the land in 1034.
claims.note: German annals hint at a split between them after Oldřich's release. Czech sources simply have Oldřich take over.

claims.text: A Vršovci man murdered Jaromír at Lysá.
claims.note: Cosmas names the killer as a Vršovci retainer. He wrote about ninety years later and hated the clan.

reigns.hook: Oldřich is home and his brother is blind. He has outlasted everyone. He has only a few months left to enjoy it.

reigns.tagline: Free again, cruel to his brother, then suddenly dead
reigns.previously: Jaromír is back, but Conrad II sets Oldřich free.
paragraphs: Oldřich came home from his Bavarian prison in 1034 and took Prague back as if he had never left. He wanted no rivals. His brother Jaromír was blinded and locked up at Lysá. He also fell out with his own son Bretislaus, who had been ruling Moravia and was driven out for a time.

Then, on 9 November 1034, Oldřich died without warning. Cosmas says it happened at dinner. People whispered about poison. The blind Jaromír was offered the throne, but he handed it to his nephew Bretislaus and told the nobles to obey him. The Vršovci clan did not forget, and the old man was murdered the next year.

claims.text: Oldřich was poisoned.
claims.note: Only rumour. Cosmas reports a sudden death at table without naming a cause.

claims.text: The blind Jaromír passed the throne to Bretislaus.
claims.note: Cosmas gives Jaromír a noble speech handing over power. Some lists still count Jaromír as duke again in 1034–1035.

reigns.hook: The brothers' war is over and both are dead or broken. Božena's son Bretislaus takes Prague, already famous for snatching his bride from a convent.

reigns.tagline: The bride thief who stole a saint from Poland
reigns.previously: Oldřich dies suddenly at table. His son Bretislaus is next.
paragraphs: Cosmas called Bretislaus (Břetislav) the Bohemian Achilles, and gave him a hero's love story. As a young man he wanted Judith, the daughter of a German count, who lived in a convent at Schweinfurt. So he rode in, snatched her and carried her off to Bohemia. Once duke, he went bigger. Around 1038 or 1039 he stormed into Poland, sacked Gniezno and carried off the bones of St Adalbert to Prague.

The German king Henry III would not tolerate that kind of power grab. In 1040 he invaded, and the Czechs ambushed and beat his army in the forests at Brůdek. Henry came back in 1041, reached Prague, and Bretislaus had to submit and give up most of what he'd taken. He stayed a loyal vassal from then on.
Before he died at Chrudim in January 1055 he set a rule: the eldest Přemyslid would always be duke. It was meant to stop civil war. It would cause a great deal of it.

claims.text: Bretislaus carried Judith off from her convent at Schweinfurt.
claims.note: Cosmas tells it with gusto, even saying he slashed through a chain on the gate. The marriage is real; the raid may be embroidered.

claims.text: He took St Adalbert's relics from Gniezno to Prague.
claims.note: Polish and Czech sources agree, and the bones were a prize Gniezno never forgave.

claims.text: He laid down that the eldest Přemyslid should always rule.
claims.note: Cosmas reports the rule. How formal it was, and what exactly it said, historians still argue.

reigns.hook: Bretislaus is dead. His eldest son Spytihněv rules for six years. Then the next brother, Vratislaus, gets his turn and dreams of a crown.

reigns.previously: Bretislaus I dies, and his eldest son takes over.
paragraphs: Spytihněv II began his reign by expelling Germans from Bohemia, including his own mother, according to the chronicler Cosmas. He kept his younger brothers on a tight leash.
He supported the reform popes, who allowed him to wear a bishop's mitre. He died young in 1061, and his brother Vratislaus took the throne.
reigns.hook: His brother Vratislaus takes over and will become Bohemia's first king.

reigns.tagline: Bohemia's first king, by the emperor's grace
reigns.previously: Spytihněv II dies after six years. His brother Vratislaus is next.
paragraphs: Vratislaus (Vratislav) took over from his brother Spytihněv II, the next in line under their father's rule of seniority. He bet his reign on one man, the emperor Henry IV. When the pope and the emperor fought over who could appoint bishops, Vratislaus stuck with Henry through every defeat. Czech knights fought in his wars in Saxony and Italy.

Loyalty paid. In 1085 Henry made him King of Bohemia, and he was crowned in Prague that June. The title was a reward for him alone, not for his sons. He moved his court to the rock of Vyšehrad and founded a church there. At home he fought his own brother Jaromír, who had become Bishop of Prague as Gebhard and was a proud, violent priest.
In January 1092 he fell from his horse while hunting and died. The crown died with him, and the seniority rule handed the duchy to his brother Conrad.

claims.text: He was made the first King of Bohemia in 1085.
claims.note: Henry IV granted the title at a synod at Mainz; the coronation in Prague followed on 15 June 1085, though Cosmas dates it 1086. It was for life only.

claims.text: The Vyšehrad Codex was made for his coronation.
claims.note: A lovely gospel book from about 1085. Tradition ties it to the coronation, but there's no proof.

claims.text: He died after falling from his horse while hunting.
claims.note: Cosmas says so. No other early source gives details.

reigns.hook: The king is dead and his crown dies with him. Under Bretislaus's old rule the duchy goes to the eldest Přemyslid alive: the king's own estranged brother, Conrad of Brno.

reigns.tagline: Eight months on the throne his brother denied him
reigns.previously: Vratislaus II, Bohemia's first king, dies after a hunting fall.
paragraphs: Conrad (Konrád) was a younger son of Bretislaus I and had spent his life as Prince of Brno in Moravia. He and his brother Vratislaus did not get on. In 1091 the king led an army to Brno to deal with him, and it took a family peace deal to end the siege.

Months later Vratislaus was dead after a hunting fall, and the old rule of seniority made Conrad, the eldest Přemyslid alive, the new duke. The crown of 1085 had been for Vratislaus alone, so Conrad was a duke again. He barely had time to settle in. He died on 6 September 1092, after about eight months, and the seniority rule jumped to the next generation.

claims.text: Conrad's wife Wirpirk pleaded with the king to spare Brno.
claims.note: Cosmas gives her a long, moving speech at the siege of 1091. The words are surely his own invention.

claims.text: Conrad became duke under the seniority rule of Bretislaus I.
claims.note: Cosmas states it, and Conrad was clearly the eldest male Přemyslid in 1092.

reigns.hook: Conrad is dead. The eldest Přemyslid is now his nephew Bretislaus, a young man who hates pagans, sorcerers and Slavonic church books.

reigns.tagline: The zealous duke struck down on a winter hunt
reigns.previously: Conrad I dies after only eight months as duke.
paragraphs: Bretislaus II was Vratislaus II's son and a man on a mission. Cosmas admired him for sweeping away the old ways: he had sacred groves burned and drove fortune tellers and sorcerers out of the land. In 1096 he expelled the monks of Sázava, the last place in Bohemia where Mass was sung in Old Church Slavonic, and put Latin monks in their place.

He also meddled with the seniority rule. He got the emperor Henry IV to recognise his younger brother Bořivoj as heir, passing over the older Moravian cousins. On 22 December 1100, at a hunting lodge near Zbečno, he was struck down in the evening dark by an assassin. Many blamed the Vršovci clan.

claims.text: Bretislaus II had pagan groves burned and sorcerers expelled.
claims.note: Cosmas, who knew him, describes it with approval. How much paganism was really left is debated.

claims.text: The Vršovci clan was behind his murder.
claims.note: Cosmas links the killer to the clan, which was blamed at the time. Nothing was ever proved.

claims.text: He drove the Slavonic-liturgy monks out of Sázava in 1096.
claims.note: The Sázava chronicle in the continuation of Cosmas records the expulsion.

reigns.hook: Bretislaus is dead in the snow. His brother Bořivoj is the named heir, but the Moravian cousins say the eldest should rule, and they are older.

reigns.tagline: The heir his brother chose, and his cousins hated
reigns.cameToPower: Named heir, backed by Henry IV
reigns.previously: Bretislaus II is murdered while out hunting.
paragraphs: Bořivoj II took Prague days after his brother's murder. He had Henry IV's blessing and his brother's nomination. What he lacked was the best claim. His cousin Oldřich of Brno, Conrad I's son, was older and said the rule of seniority made him duke. In 1101 Oldřich marched on Bohemia, but Bořivoj saw him off.

The next challenger was harder. Svatopluk of Olomouc, another Moravian cousin, was ruthless and hungry. Bořivoj's own nobles began to drift towards him. In May 1107 Svatopluk's friends opened Prague to him, and Bořivoj had to run. He would spend years trying to get back.

claims.text: Oldřich of Brno invaded in 1101 to claim the duchy by seniority.
claims.note: Cosmas describes the campaign and its failure.

claims.text: Traitors inside Prague let Svatopluk in.
claims.note: Cosmas blames treachery among Bořivoj's own men. He was close to events but not neutral.

reigns.hook: Svatopluk of Olomouc holds Prague. He is clever, brave and merciless, and he has a score to settle with the Vršovci clan.

reigns.tagline: The cousin who wiped out a clan and died for it
reigns.previously: His cousin Svatopluk of Olomouc drives Bořivoj II out of Prague.
paragraphs: Svatopluk was a Moravian prince, the son of Otto of Olomouc and a grandson of Bretislaus I. He had no claim by seniority, so he took Prague the other way. In 1107 he turned up with an army and friends among the Czech nobles, and Bořivoj II fled. Among the men who helped him were the Vršovci, the most powerful clan in the country.

That help did not save them. In 1108 Svatopluk had the Vršovci rounded up and killed across Bohemia. Cosmas, who saw it, was shocked by the bloodshed. Svatopluk also had to keep the young emperor Henry V happy, so he marched in Henry's wars against Hungary and then Poland. In September 1109, in the imperial camp near Głogów, an assassin struck him down. He died where he fell.

claims.text: Svatopluk had the Vršovci clan massacred in 1108.
claims.note: Cosmas lived through it and describes the killings in detail. The clan had long rivalled the dukes.

claims.text: His killer was a Vršovci man taking revenge for the massacre.
claims.note: Cosmas links the assassin to the clan, but who sent him was never settled. Some suspected Svatopluk's Czech rivals.

reigns.hook: Svatopluk lies dead in the emperor's camp. The Czech army picks Bořivoj's younger brother Vladislaus on the spot. Bořivoj has other ideas.

reigns.tagline: The brother who won the throne, then gave it back
reigns.cameToPower: Chosen by the army, backed by Henry V
reigns.reignEnded: Handed the throne back to Bořivoj
reigns.previously: Svatopluk is murdered in the emperor's camp near Głogów.
paragraphs: Vladislaus (Vladislav) was the son of King Vratislaus II and the younger brother of Bořivoj II. The Czech troops at Głogów chose him as soon as Svatopluk fell. Bořivoj rushed back and grabbed Prague, so the brothers went to war. Vladislaus called in Henry V. In early 1110 the emperor came to Bohemia, seized Bořivoj and sent him off as a prisoner to Germany.

That left another brother. Soběslav, the youngest, fled to Poland, and Bolesław III of Poland invaded on his behalf in 1110. Vladislaus held on. He kept on good terms with the emperor, and that mattered more than anything. Then, in 1117, he stepped down and let Bořivoj come back. Nobody at the time wrote down why.

claims.text: Henry V took Bořivoj II prisoner and held him in Germany.
claims.note: Cosmas reports it. Bořivoj was kept in a German castle for several years.

claims.text: Vladislaus gave the throne back in 1117 of his own free will.
claims.note: The sources record the handover but not the reason. He may have kept part of the land for himself.

reigns.hook: In 1117 Vladislaus does what no Přemyslid ever does: he hands over Prague. His brother Bořivoj, back from captivity, is duke again. For now.

reigns.tagline: Duke again, three years on borrowed time
reigns.previously: Vladislaus I gives the throne back to his brother Bořivoj.
paragraphs: Bořivoj II had already been thrown out twice, first by his cousin Svatopluk and then by his own brother. Now, after years as the emperor's prisoner, he sat on the throne in Prague again. Nobody quite knows why Vladislaus let him. The best guess is a family deal, perhaps with the land split between them.

If it was a deal, it did not last. In 1120 Vladislaus took Prague back by force, and this time Bořivoj never returned. He went into exile in Hungary and died there on 2 February 1124. Three times duke of Bohemia, he ended his days as a guest in a foreign land.

claims.text: Bořivoj and Vladislaus may have shared the country between 1117 and 1120.
claims.note: Cosmas is short on detail for these years. Some historians read his words as a split, others as a plain handover.

claims.text: Bořivoj II died in exile in Hungary in 1124.
claims.note: Cosmas gives the date. He never got back into Bohemia after 1120.

reigns.hook: Bořivoj is gone for good. Vladislaus is back, and this time he means to keep the throne. But his youngest brother Soběslav is still waiting his turn.

reigns.tagline: One last reign and a deathbed peace
reigns.previously: Vladislaus throws his brother Bořivoj out of Prague for good.
paragraphs: Back on the throne, Vladislaus spent his last years keeping his family in line. His sharpest rival now was his youngest brother Soběslav, who held lands in Moravia and wanted more. The two fell out, and Soběslav was driven into exile. Vladislaus leaned instead towards his Moravian cousin Otto of Olomouc as his heir.

Their mother Svatava was still alive, a Polish princess and the widow of King Vratislaus II. As Vladislaus lay dying in spring 1125, she brought her sons together. Soběslav came home and was named the next duke. Vladislaus died on 12 April 1125 and was buried at Kladruby, the abbey he had founded in 1115. His own son, another Vladislaus, would one day be king.

claims.text: Their mother Svatava reconciled the brothers as Vladislaus was dying.
claims.note: Cosmas tells the scene, and he was writing at the time. Some historians think he made it more touching than it was.

claims.text: Vladislaus had favoured Otto of Olomouc as his successor.
claims.note: Cosmas and the later annals agree Otto expected the throne. It is why he turned to the emperor next.

reigns.hook: Vladislaus dies with Soběslav as heir. But Otto of Olomouc thinks the throne was promised to him, and the new German king Lothair agrees.

reigns.tagline: The duke who trapped a German king in the snow
reigns.cameToPower: Named heir as his brother died
reigns.previously: Vladislaus I dies, at peace at last with his brother Soběslav.
paragraphs: Soběslav was the last of Vratislaus II's sons to rule. He had barely sat down when Otto the Black of Olomouc went to Lothair III, the new German king, and talked him into an invasion. In February 1126 Lothair crossed the border hills with a small army. At Chlumec the Czechs caught it in the snow and cut it to pieces. Otto was killed. Lothair, surrounded, had to make peace and hand Bohemia to Soběslav as a fief.

After that the two got on well, and Soběslav fought loyally for Lothair. At home he was tough with rebels and kept the peace. He was also the first duke the old priest Cosmas did not live to write about: the chronicler died in October 1125, his book finished. Soběslav spent his last years trying to make his own son, also called Vladislaus, the next duke, and made the nobles swear to it.

claims.text: Soběslav beat Lothair III at Chlumec on 18 February 1126.
claims.note: Czech and German chroniclers both record it. It is one of very few Czech wins over a German king in person.

claims.text: St Adalbert's banner flew on St Wenceslas's spear at Chlumec, and the saint himself was seen over the Czech ranks.
claims.note: A story from the continuation of Cosmas by the Monk of Sázava. The spear and banner were real relics; the vision is pious tradition.

reigns.hook: Soběslav dies sure his son will follow. Behind his back the nobles pick a different Vladislaus: the son of Vladislaus I.

reigns.tagline: A crown from Barbarossa and a bridge for his queen
reigns.previously: Soběslav I dies. The nobles pass over his son.
paragraphs: This Vladislaus (Vladislav) is the first of two Vladislaus IIs in Czech history; the other is a Polish prince three centuries later. Elected by the nobles in 1140, he soon learned what they thought of him. In 1142 the princes of Moravia rose, beat his army and besieged Prague. He held on with help from the German king. In 1147 he went on the Second Crusade.

His big moment came with Frederick Barbarossa. The emperor needed troops to crush Milan, and in January 1158 at Regensburg he made Vladislaus a king in return. Czech knights fought hard in Italy. Back home, Prague got its first stone bridge across the Vltava, named the Judith Bridge after his queen. It stood until a flood wrecked it in 1342.
Old and tired, in 1172 he handed Bohemia to his son Frederick without asking the emperor. Barbarossa was furious. Vladislaus died in exile in Thuringia in 1174.

claims.text: Barbarossa crowned him king in exchange for help against Milan.
claims.note: Vincent of Prague, who went to Italy with Bishop Daniel of Prague, tells the story in detail.

claims.text: He abdicated in 1172.
claims.note: Some sources date the handover to 1173. Either way, the emperor was not consulted.

claims.text: The bridge was named after Queen Judith because she paid for it.
claims.note: The name is old; who funded it is not recorded for certain.

reigns.hook: The old king hands Bohemia to his son Frederick without asking Barbarossa. The crown lapses, and the emperor is about to show who really picks Bohemia's dukes.

reigns.tagline: The son who got his father's job and the emperor's anger
reigns.previously: Vladislaus II hands Bohemia to his son without asking the emperor.
paragraphs: Frederick (Bedřich in Czech) was King Vladislaus II's eldest son by his first wife, Gertrude of Babenberg. He was married to Elizabeth, a daughter of King Géza II of Hungary. His father gave him the duchy in 1172 and retired. The royal crown did not pass with it. It had been granted to Vladislaus alone.

There was one problem. Nobody had asked Frederick Barbarossa, and the emperor saw Bohemia as his to hand out. In 1173 he summoned the Přemyslids, refused to accept Frederick and gave the duchy to the sons of Soběslav I instead. Frederick had to go, and his father went into exile, where he died the next year.

claims.text: Barbarossa threw Frederick out because his father had not asked imperial permission.
claims.note: German and Czech annals agree the emperor treated the abdication as a challenge to his right to grant the duchy.

claims.text: Vladislaus II handed over power in 1172.
claims.note: Some sources date the handover to 1173. Either way, Frederick's first spell was short.

reigns.hook: Barbarossa won't have Frederick. The man he picks has spent years locked up in the castle of Přimda: Soběslav, son of Soběslav I.

reigns.tagline: From the dungeon to the throne, beloved by the poor
reigns.previously: Barbarossa refuses Frederick and hands Bohemia to Soběslav's sons.
paragraphs: Soběslav II had been robbed of the throne once already, as a boy in 1140. Under Vladislaus II he kept trying to win it back and ended up a prisoner in the castle of Přimda, near the Bavarian border. Barbarossa's decision of 1173 got him out. Within weeks the prisoner was duke.

He was an odd duke. The great nobles disliked him and he did not much like them. Ordinary people, the story goes, found him fair, and he earned the nickname 'Prince of the Peasants'. He gave the German merchants of Prague their own rights and law. He also raided Austria, and by 1178 the emperor had turned against him. In 1178 Frederick came back with imperial backing, and Soběslav fled. He died in exile on 29 January 1180.

claims.text: He was called 'Prince of the Peasants' because he protected ordinary people.
claims.note: The nickname is old, but the stories behind it come from later chroniclers. It may have started as a noble sneer.

claims.text: He granted the Germans of Prague their own law.
claims.note: The privilege of Soběslav II for the Prague Germans is usually dated 1174 to 1178. It is known from a later confirmation.

reigns.hook: Soběslav is on the run. Frederick rides back into Prague with the emperor's blessing. The nobles, though, have not finished picking dukes for themselves.

reigns.tagline: Back in Prague, while the emperor carves up the country
reigns.previously: Soběslav II flees. Frederick is duke of Bohemia again.
paragraphs: Frederick's second spell was longer but no calmer. In 1182 the Czech nobles rose against him and chose Conrad Otto, a Moravian Přemyslid. Frederick fled to Barbarossa. The emperor called both sides to Regensburg, put Frederick back and gave the nobles a fright. He also made Moravia a separate margraviate under the empire, with Conrad Otto as margrave.

Fighting went on. In December 1185 Frederick's brother Ottokar beat Conrad Otto at Loděnice in a bloody battle. A peace made at Knín in 1186 settled that Conrad Otto would follow Frederick. Barbarossa chipped away again in 1187, making the Bishop of Prague a prince of the empire in his own right. Frederick died on 25 March 1189.

claims.text: Barbarossa made Moravia a separate margraviate in 1182.
claims.note: Recorded in German and Czech annals. It took Moravia out of Prague's direct control for a time.

claims.text: The battle of Loděnice in 1185 was one of the bloodiest of the age.
claims.note: Gerlach of Mühlhausen describes heavy losses on both sides. His figures can't be checked.

reigns.hook: Frederick dies in March 1189. Under the deal struck at Knín, the duchy now passes to his old enemy, Conrad Otto of Moravia.

reigns.tagline: The lawmaker duke who died at the gates of Naples
reigns.reignEnded: Plague at the siege of Naples
reigns.previously: Frederick dies. Conrad Otto of Moravia becomes duke of Bohemia.
paragraphs: Conrad Otto (Konrád Ota) came from the Znojmo branch of the Přemyslids. Now he was Duke of Bohemia and Margrave of Moravia at once, so the Czech lands were back in one pair of hands. In 1189 he issued the Statutes of Conrad, which wrote down the rights of the Czech nobility. They are often called the first Czech law code.

He did not get long to use them. In 1191 he led Czech troops for the new emperor Henry VI on his march to take southern Italy. The army sat down to besiege Naples in the summer heat, and disease tore through the camp. Conrad Otto died there on 9 September 1191, a long way from Prague.

claims.text: The Statutes of Conrad (1189) are the first written law code of the Czech nobility.
claims.note: They are the oldest grant of noble rights to survive, but the text we have may have been confirmed or reworded later.

claims.text: He died of plague at the siege of Naples.
claims.note: German chroniclers report that disease ruined Henry VI's army at Naples and name Conrad among the dead.

reigns.hook: Conrad Otto dies far from home. In Prague the throne goes to an old man few expected: Wenceslaus, last surviving son of Soběslav I.

reigns.tagline: An old man's turn, over within months
reigns.previously: Conrad Otto dies of plague outside Naples.
paragraphs: This Wenceslaus (Václav) is easy to mix up, so to be clear: he was a duke for a few months in 1191 and 1192, not the famous King Wenceslaus II who ruled a century later, from 1278 to 1305. He was a son of Soběslav I and a younger brother of Soběslav II, and by now in his fifties.

He had no army of his own worth the name and no friend at the emperor's court. Ottokar, Vladislaus II's son, did. With the help of his cousin Henry Bretislaus, Bishop of Prague, Ottokar got Henry VI to grant him Bohemia, and Wenceslaus was pushed out in 1192. No one wrote down where he died, or when.

claims.text: He was the brother of Soběslav II and the son of Soběslav I.
claims.note: The Prague annals name him in that line. Little else about him is recorded.

claims.text: Ottokar bought Bohemia from Henry VI for 6,000 marks.
claims.note: Gerlach of Mühlhausen gives the sum. Whether it was ever paid in full is another matter.

reigns.hook: Wenceslaus is gone. The new duke, Ottokar, has bought Bohemia from the emperor on credit. The bill is huge, and the emperor wants it paid.

reigns.tagline: He bought the duchy on credit and couldn't pay
reigns.previously: Old Duke Wenceslaus is pushed out within months.
paragraphs: Ottokar (Přemysl Otakar) was a younger son of King Vladislaus II and his second wife, Judith of Thuringia. He had already led his brother Frederick's army to victory at Loděnice in 1185. In 1192 he finally got Bohemia for himself, with a promise of a fortune in silver to the emperor Henry VI.

The money never came. Instead Ottokar joined a plot of German princes against Henry VI. The emperor took the duchy back in 1193 and gave it to Ottokar's cousin, Henry Bretislaus, the Bishop of Prague. Ottokar would not let go without a fight, but he lost. He went into exile and spent the next four years waiting for his luck to turn.

claims.text: Ottokar promised Henry VI 6,000 marks of silver for Bohemia.
claims.note: The sum comes from Gerlach of Mühlhausen. Other sources give no figure.

claims.text: Henry VI deposed him for joining the princes' conspiracy.
claims.note: German annals tie his fall to the revolt of 1192 to 1193. Not paying cannot have helped.

reigns.hook: Henry VI has picked a new duke: Henry Bretislaus, Bishop of Prague, a Přemyslid in a mitre. Ottokar won't leave quietly.

reigns.tagline: A bishop with a sword: Prague's priest-duke
reigns.previously: Ottokar can't pay the emperor, and Henry VI throws him out.
paragraphs: Henry Bretislaus, Jindřich Břetislav in Czech, was a grandson of Duke Vladislaus I and had been Bishop of Prague since 1182. He spent years fighting the dukes over who owned the Church's lands and men, and he won. In 1187 Barbarossa made him a prince of the empire in his own right, answerable only to the emperor, over the head of the duke in Prague.

In 1193 Emperor Henry VI went further and gave him Bohemia itself. Ottokar would not leave quietly, so the bishop came with an army and drove him out. For four years one man held the crozier and the duke's banner at once, the only Přemyslid ever to do so.
By 1197 he was ill. He went to Cheb on the western border, and he died there on 15 June 1197. The nobles had to pick a new duke fast, before Ottokar came back.

claims.text: Henry Bretislaus was the only man to rule Bohemia as bishop and duke at the same time.
claims.note: Gerlach of Mühlhausen, abbot of Milevsko and a contemporary, records his double rule; no other Bishop of Prague ever held the duchy.

claims.text: He held Ottokar's brother Vladislaus Henry prisoner for a time.
claims.note: Some accounts say the bishop captured him during the fighting of the 1190s. The details are thin and the dates are unclear.

reigns.hook: The bishop-duke is dead. The nobles choose Ottokar's younger brother, Vladislaus Henry. But the emperor dies in Sicily that September, and Ottokar is already marching home.

reigns.tagline: The duke who gave his throne to his brother
reigns.previously: Bishop-duke Henry Bretislaus dies at Cheb. Prague needs a duke.
paragraphs: Vladislaus Henry, Vladislav Jindřich in Czech, was a son of King Vladislaus II, and Bohemian lists count him Duke Vladislaus III. The nobles chose him in summer 1197. He had six months. In September Emperor Henry VI died at Messina, and the empire's grip on Bohemia went slack. Ottokar, the elder brother, had been waiting in exile for exactly this.

In December Ottokar marched on Prague. The brothers' armies faced each other, and then the two men talked. On 6 December 1197 they settled it: Ottokar took Bohemia, and Vladislaus Henry took Moravia as margrave. He kept that deal for 25 years. He stayed loyal to his brother, and in 1205 he helped found the Cistercian abbey of Velehrad. He died as margrave in 1222.

claims.text: The brothers settled the throne without a battle on 6 December 1197.
claims.note: Gerlach of Mühlhausen, writing at the time, describes the meeting and the deal. After decades of blindings and murders, it stood out.

claims.text: Vladislaus Henry co-founded Velehrad Abbey in Moravia.
claims.note: The abbey's foundation charters name him with Bishop Robert of Olomouc; the monks arrived about 1205.

reigns.hook: Ottokar finally has Bohemia. Germany has two rival kings, both desperate for friends. A clever duke could sell himself for a crown.

reigns.tagline: The turncoat duke who made Bohemia a kingdom for good
reigns.previously: Vladislaus Henry swaps Bohemia for Moravia. Ottokar is back in Prague.
paragraphs: Ottokar, Přemysl Otakar in Czech, had been duke once before and lost the job within a year. Second time round he played it smarter. In 1198 Germany had two rival kings, Philip of Swabia and Otto of Brunswick, and both needed friends. Ottokar backed Philip, who crowned him king. When Otto looked like the better bet, Ottokar switched sides. Then he switched again. Each time the price was the same: recognise my crown.

Earlier kings of Bohemia got the title for life only. Ottokar wanted it nailed down. In 1212 the young Frederick II, desperate for allies, issued the Golden Bull of Sicily. It confirmed the royal title for Ottokar's heirs and let the Czechs choose their own king. At home he dumped his first wife, Adela of Meissen, to marry Constance of Hungary, and fought Adela's family and the Pope over it for years.

He also killed off the old seniority rule, where the eldest Přemyslid inherited and brothers and cousins fought over it. Instead he had his own son Wenceslaus crowned in 1228, while he was still alive. When Ottokar died two years later, nobody argued.

claims.text: The Golden Bull of Sicily made the Bohemian crown hereditary.
claims.note: The charter, issued at Basel in September 1212 and sealed with the gold seal of Frederick II as King of Sicily, survives in Prague.

claims.text: Ottokar changed sides in the German civil war at least twice.
claims.note: Chronicles and charters show him with Philip, then Otto, then Philip's camp again. Historians see it as cold calculation.

claims.text: Ottokar divorced Adela because they were too closely related.
claims.note: That was the legal excuse offered to the Church. Most historians think he simply wanted the Hungarian alliance that came with Constance.

reigns.hook: The old fox dies with his heir already crowned. But the new king, Wenceslaus, has only one good eye, and out east a storm is building on the steppe.

reigns.tagline: The one-eyed king who loved knights, songs and hunting
reigns.previously: Ottokar I dies, with his son Wenceslaus already crowned king.
paragraphs: Don't mix him up with the saint. This Wenceslaus, Václav in Czech, ruled three hundred years later and wore a real king's crown. He lost an eye as a young man, and he lived for the hunt and the tournament. German poets sang at his court, and German settlers poured in to clear forests, dig mines and found new walled towns with their own laws.

In 1241 the Mongols smashed the Poles and Germans at Legnica in Silesia. Wenceslaus was marching to help and arrived too late, then held the border. His eldest son died young in 1247, and the next one, Ottokar, did not wait his turn: he led a noble revolt in 1248 and called himself the younger king. Wenceslaus beat him, forgave him and sent him off to grab Austria.

His sister Agnes turned down royal suitors, maybe even an emperor, and founded a convent of Poor Clares and a hospital in Prague. Wenceslaus died in September 1253, and the rebel son walked in as king.

claims.text: Wenceslaus lost his eye in a hunting accident.
claims.note: That's the usual story, but no contemporary explains how it happened. Chroniclers only note that he was one-eyed.

claims.text: The Bohemian army was just a day's march short of Legnica.
claims.note: Later chronicles say so, and it makes a dramatic near-miss. How close the army really was is uncertain.

claims.text: Agnes's canonisation in November 1989 freed the nation.
claims.note: An old prophecy said good things would come to Bohemia when Agnes was made a saint. She was canonised on 12 November 1989; the Velvet Revolution began five days later.

reigns.hook: The rebel son is now king, and he is already Duke of Austria. He has silver, an army and an appetite for much more.

reigns.tagline: Iron in battle, gold in the treasury, dead on the Marchfeld
reigns.previously: Wenceslaus I dies at Počaply. His rebel son Ottokar takes the crown.
paragraphs: Ottokar II, Přemysl Otakar II, wanted it all. To get Austria he married Margaret of Babenberg, the last of its old ruling family and decades older than him. In 1260 he crushed Béla IV of Hungary at Kressenbrunn and took Styria, then swapped Margaret for Béla's young granddaughter. Later came Carinthia and Carniola. His lands now ran from the Giant Mountains to the Adriatic.

He was called the Iron and Golden King: iron for his armies, gold for the silver flowing out of mines like Jihlava. He went crusading with the Teutonic Knights against the pagan Prussians, and a fort there took his name. In 1273 the German electors passed him over for a modest Swabian count, Rudolf of Habsburg. Ottokar refused to bow.

Rudolf took Austria off him in 1276. Two years later Ottokar marched back, and on 26 August 1278 he lost the battle of the Marchfeld near Dürnkrut. He was killed on the field, stripped, and his body was put on show in Vienna. His heir was six years old.

claims.text: Königsberg, now Kaliningrad, was named in Ottokar's honour.
claims.note: The Teutonic Knights founded it during his 1255 crusade and the name means King's Mountain. Most historians accept the link to Ottokar, though no founding charter spells it out.

claims.text: Ottokar was murdered after the battle by Austrian knights with a grudge.
claims.note: Austrian and Czech chroniclers say personal enemies cut him down once he was captured or unhorsed. Details differ from source to source.

claims.text: Dante put Ottokar in Purgatory, comforting his old enemy Rudolf.
claims.note: In Purgatorio, canto VII, the two rivals sit side by side in the valley of negligent princes.

reigns.hook: Ottokar's body is on display in Vienna. In Prague a six-year-old boy is king, and his guardian is about to lock him in a castle.

reigns.tagline: Kidnapped boy, silver king, ruler of two crowns
reigns.previously: Ottokar II dies on the Marchfeld. His heir is a boy of six.
paragraphs: Young Wenceslaus spent his first years as king as a prisoner. His guardian, Otto of Brandenburg, shut him up in Bezděz castle and then carried him off to Brandenburg, while Otto's men plundered Bohemia. He came home in 1283. His mother's lover, the nobleman Záviš of Falkenstein, then ran the kingdom and married her. When Wenceslaus grew up he had Záviš arrested, and in 1290 beheaded in front of Hluboká castle to force its surrender.

Then came the silver. A huge strike at Kutná Hora made him one of the richest kings in Europe. In 1300 he launched the Prague groschen, a heavy silver coin that was used across central Europe, and issued a mining code to go with it. That same year he was crowned King of Poland at Gniezno, and in 1301 his young son was crowned King of Hungary.
The Habsburg king Albert I invaded in 1304 but gave up in front of Kutná Hora. Wenceslaus did not get to enjoy it. Long ill, he died in Prague in June 1305, aged only 33.

claims.text: Wenceslaus II wrote love songs in German.
claims.note: The Codex Manesse includes three songs under the name King Wenceslas of Bohemia. Most scholars credit him, but some think they belong to his grandfather Wenceslaus I.

claims.text: He was a pious, gentle king, a fan of monks and books.
claims.note: That's the picture in the Chronicle of Zbraslav. Its abbot-authors owed him their monastery, so they were hardly neutral.

claims.text: Záviš was beheaded below Hluboká to make the garrison give up.
claims.note: The Chronicle of Zbraslav reports it. The castle was held by Záviš's kinsmen.

reigns.hook: The silver king is dead at 33. His only son is fifteen, wild, and wearing two foreign crowns he cannot hold.

reigns.tagline: Last of the Přemyslids, stabbed at sixteen
reigns.previously: Wenceslaus II dies in Prague. His only son is fifteen.
paragraphs: At eleven Wenceslaus had been crowned King of Hungary under the name Ladislaus. It never took. His father brought him home in 1304, and once on the Bohemian throne the boy handed the Hungarian claim to Otto of Bavaria. He still called himself King of Poland, though, and Poland was slipping away to the Piast duke Władysław the Elbow-high.

The chroniclers paint him as a wild teenager who drank, partied and gave away royal property to his friends. Maybe. What we know is that in summer 1306 he raised an army to win Poland back. On 4 August, resting in Olomouc in Moravia, he was stabbed to death in his lodgings.
Nobody ever proved who did it, or who paid. With him died the last male Přemyslid, from a family that had ruled the Czechs for over four hundred years.

claims.text: A Thuringian knight called Konrad of Botenstein was the killer.
claims.note: Some chroniclers name him and say he was cut down on the spot, so he could not be questioned. Others don't name anyone.

claims.text: The murder was ordered by the Habsburgs, Władysław or rebel Czech nobles.
claims.note: All three had motives and all three have been blamed. There is no evidence that settles it.

claims.text: Wenceslaus spent his short reign drinking and giving away crown lands.
claims.note: The Chronicle of Zbraslav and Dalimil say so, but young kings who died early often got this treatment.

reigns.hook: The Přemyslids are gone. Two princesses are left. The eldest's husband, Henry of Carinthia, moves fast for the crown, but the German king Albert of Habsburg wants it for his son.

reigns.tagline: The Carinthian who got there first, then ran
reigns.cameToPower: Elected by part of the nobles
reigns.reignEnded: Driven out by Albert I's army
reigns.previously: Wenceslaus III is stabbed at Olomouc. The Přemyslids are gone.
paragraphs: Henry was Duke of Carinthia and Count of Tyrol, from the Alpine house of Gorizia-Tyrol. His claim to Prague came through his wife Anne, the eldest daughter of Wenceslaus II. Within weeks of the murder at Olomouc, a party of Czech nobles chose him as king, and he hurried to Prague.

The German king, Albert I of Habsburg, had other plans. He said Bohemia was an empty fief of the empire, and he meant to give it to his eldest son Rudolf. This was a family fight: Albert's wife Elisabeth was Henry's sister, so Henry was being pushed out by his brother-in-law in favour of his own nephew. Albert's army marched in. Henry had little money and fewer friends, and by October he had left Bohemia.

claims.text: Albert I was Henry's brother-in-law, so Rudolf was Henry's nephew.
claims.note: Albert married Elisabeth, daughter of Meinhard II of Gorizia-Tyrol, Henry's father. The family ties are well documented.

claims.text: The Chronicle of Dalimil was written to back Henry's cause.
claims.note: The verse chronicle praises Henry and rails against Germans, and many scholars link its author to Henry's party. Who wrote it, and why, is unknown.

reigns.hook: Henry is gone. Albert's son Rudolf rides into Prague, already Duke of Austria at about 25. He has a plan to make the crown stick: marry the dead king's widow.

reigns.tagline: The thrifty Habsburg the Czechs called King Porridge
reigns.reignEnded: Died of dysentery at a siege
reigns.previously: Albert I's army marches in. Henry of Carinthia runs for home.
paragraphs: Rudolf was the eldest son of the German king Albert I, and already Duke of Austria. The Bohemian estates accepted him as king in autumn 1306, and on 16 October he married Elisabeth Richeza, Wenceslaus II's young widow, to tie himself to the old dynasty. Like the Přemyslids before him he also called himself King of Poland. His father made sure that Rudolf's brothers were named as his heirs.

Rudolf tried to pay off the crown's debts and claw back royal land, and he kept a frugal court. The nobles mocked him as King Porridge. Some went into open revolt. In summer 1307 he besieged the rebel lord Bavor of Strakonice at Horažďovice, and dysentery swept his camp. He died there on 3 or 4 July 1307, after less than a year as king, and he was buried in St Vitus Cathedral.

claims.text: The Czechs called Rudolf "King Porridge" (král Kaše).
claims.note: The nickname comes from Czech chronicle tradition. Whether it mocked his thrift, his plain food or his weakness is not clear.

claims.text: Rudolf died on 4 July 1307.
claims.note: Sources split between 3 and 4 July. Everyone agrees it was dysentery, caught at the siege of Horažďovice.

claims.text: Rudolf is buried in St Vitus Cathedral in Prague.
claims.note: His tomb is in the cathedral's royal burial places, a Habsburg among Přemyslids.

reigns.hook: Rudolf is dead, and his brother Frederick says the crown is his by the deal. The Czech nobles have other ideas. They want Henry of Carinthia back.

reigns.tagline: Back on the throne, broke and never crowned
reigns.previously: Rudolf dies of dysentery at a siege. The throne is empty again.
paragraphs: On 15 August 1307 the nobles elected Henry again and passed over Rudolf's brother Frederick the Fair. Albert I invaded once more that autumn and got nowhere. In May 1308 Albert was murdered by his own nephew, and the Habsburgs gave up their claim for cash. Henry had the throne to himself.

He never managed to be crowned. He was short of money, the barons ignored him, and the German townsmen and the Czech lords were at each other's throats. A group of nobles and Cistercian abbots decided they needed someone better. Wenceslaus III's younger sister Elizabeth was still unmarried, and the new German king, Henry VII of Luxembourg, had a teenage son. On 1 September 1310 John and Elizabeth were married at Speyer.
John's army reached Prague, and on 3 December 1310 the city let him in. Henry slipped back to Carinthia and Tyrol. He went on calling himself King of Bohemia until he died in 1335.

claims.text: Henry used the title King of Bohemia for the rest of his life.
claims.note: His later charters and seals still carry the royal title. He never gave up the claim, though he never came back.

claims.text: Henry tried to marry Elizabeth off to a minor German lord to keep her out of the game.
claims.note: The Chronicle of Zbraslav, written by the abbots who backed John, tells it this way. They had every reason to make Henry look bad.

claims.text: Albert I was murdered by his nephew in 1308.
claims.note: John, later called Parricida, killed him on 1 May 1308 over a withheld inheritance.

reigns.tagline: The absent knight-king who died charging blind
reigns.previously: John of Luxembourg's army takes Prague. Henry of Carinthia flees.
paragraphs: John was the son of Emperor Henry VII, and he loved jousting, Paris and Italian adventures much more than Prague. The Czechs called him the foreign king. To win over the nobles he gave them sweeping rights, and they ran the kingdom while he was away, which was most of the time. He fell out badly with Queen Elizabeth and took their small son Wenceslaus away from her.

Still, he was good at collecting land. He gained Cheb, Upper Lusatia and the homage of most of the Silesian dukes, and in 1335 Poland gave up its claim to Silesia. He paid with his health. From about 1340 an eye disease left him blind.
Blind or not, he went to war for his ally the King of France. At Crécy on 26 August 1346, with the battle lost, he asked his knights to lead him into the fight. He was killed, and so were they.

claims.text: John's knights tied their horses to his so they could lead him into battle.
claims.note: The story comes from the chronicler Jean Froissart, writing decades later. The bodies were reportedly found together, but the rope detail may be his.

claims.text: The Black Prince took John's ostrich feathers and motto Ich dien.
claims.note: The Prince of Wales's badge still uses three feathers and Ich dien. The idea that they came from John is a much later tradition with no solid proof.

claims.text: The Czechs nicknamed John the foreign king.
claims.note: Czech chroniclers and historians of the time complained about his long absences and his foreign favourites.

reigns.hook: John is dead at Crécy. His son was there too, wounded, and has already been elected King of the Romans. The boy John took from his mother is coming home to rule.

reigns.tagline: The emperor who turned Prague into the capital of Europe
reigns.previously: Blind King John dies at Crécy. His son Charles fought there too.
paragraphs: He was baptised Wenceslaus, Václav, after his Přemyslid ancestors. Sent to the French court at seven, he took the name Charles there. Back home as a young man, he found the royal castles falling apart and had to relearn his Czech. When his father fell at Crécy, Charles had already been elected King of the Romans that July.

Then he built. Prague got an archbishop in 1344. In 1348 Charles founded the first university in central Europe and a whole New Town. He built Karlštejn castle to guard the crown jewels and relics, started a stone bridge over the Vltava in 1357, and hired Peter Parler to finish St Vitus Cathedral. He was crowned emperor in Rome in 1355.

His Golden Bull of 1356 fixed how emperors were chosen and made the King of Bohemia the first lay elector. He even wrote his own life story. Before he died in 1378, he made sure his son Wenceslaus was already crowned and elected.

claims.text: Charles Bridge was begun at 5:31 on 9 July 1357, making the palindrome 135797531.
claims.note: The date fits the records, but the minute-perfect palindrome only appears in later accounts. An astrologer's choice is a nice story with no proof.

claims.text: The Hunger Wall was built to give the poor of Prague paid work.
claims.note: The wall on Petřín Hill was a real defence work of the 1360s. The job-creation story is later tradition.

claims.text: Czechs voted Charles IV the greatest Czech of all time.
claims.note: He won Czech Television's poll in 2005. The fictional genius Jára Cimrman got more votes but was ruled out.

reigns.hook: The great emperor is dead, and the crown goes to his son Wenceslaus. He is seventeen and was raised to rule, but he is about to find it very hard.

reigns.tagline: Jailed twice, deposed once, and Prague in revolt
reigns.previously: Charles IV dies in Prague. His son Wenceslaus is already king.
paragraphs: Wenceslaus IV was crowned King of Bohemia at two and inherited everything at seventeen. Then it went wrong. He fought the Archbishop of Prague, and in 1393 his men tortured the archbishop's vicar, John of Nepomuk, and threw him off the bridge into the Vltava. His own nobles locked him up in 1394. In 1400 the German electors deposed him as King of the Romans, and in 1402 his brother Sigismund seized him and held him in Austria.

Meanwhile a preacher named Jan Hus was packing the Bethlehem Chapel in Prague, attacking corrupt clergy. In 1409 Wenceslaus gave the Czechs control of Prague University, and the German masters walked out. Hus went to the Council of Constance under Sigismund's safe conduct and was burned there on 6 July 1415.
Prague boiled. On 30 July 1419 a Hussite crowd stormed the New Town Hall and threw the councillors out of the windows. Two and a half weeks later Wenceslaus was dead.

claims.text: John of Nepomuk died for refusing to reveal the queen's confession.
claims.note: This story appears decades later. The real quarrel was over church appointments. The legend made him a saint and his statue stands on Charles Bridge.

claims.text: Wenceslaus died of rage at the news of the defenestration.
claims.note: Chroniclers say the news threw him into a fury and he suffered a stroke soon after. The link is likely but impossible to prove.

claims.text: The electors deposed him for being useless and idle.
claims.note: Their decree of August 1400 at Oberlahnstein called him useless and negligent. The nickname the Idle grew out of that reputation.

reigns.hook: The king is dead and Prague is in revolt. His heir is Sigismund, the brother the Hussites blame for Hus's death. They aren't going to let him in.

reigns.title: The Hussite Revolution
reigns.tagline: Farmers, flails and war wagons against half of Europe
reigns.previously: Wenceslaus IV dies weeks after Prague's first defenestration.
paragraphs: When Wenceslaus died in August 1419, Bohemia was already boiling. Followers of the burned preacher Jan Hus wanted a poorer, cleaner Church and the communion cup for ordinary people as well as priests. Their programme became the Four Articles of Prague. The heir, Sigismund, was the man they blamed for Hus's death. In 1420 the Pope proclaimed a crusade, and Sigismund marched on Prague with knights from all over Europe.

The Hussites had a secret weapon: Jan Žižka, a minor knight with one eye. He turned farm carts into rolling forts, chained in a ring and bristling with handguns and flails. On 14 July 1420 his small force held Vítkov Hill above Prague and the crusade fell apart. Radicals built a new town on a hill in the south and called it Tábor. Žižka lost his other eye in 1421 and kept winning anyway, until he fell ill and died in 1424.

Four more crusades came and went. At Domažlice in 1431 the crusaders ran before the fighting really started. Hussite armies under Prokop the Bald raided deep into Germany, and in 1433 one even reached the Baltic. But war wore the country out. On 30 May 1434 an alliance of moderate and Catholic lords smashed the radical armies at Lipany, and Prokop died there. Peace terms called the Compacts let the Czechs keep the cup, and on 23 August 1436 Sigismund rode into Prague as king.

claims.text: The crusaders at Domažlice fled when they heard the Hussites singing their battle hymn, “Ye Who Are Warriors of God”.
claims.note: The hymn was real and the rout was real. Chroniclers made the singing the cause; the rumble of the approaching wagons and poor leadership mattered at least as much.

claims.text: The dying Žižka ordered his skin made into a drum, so he could keep scaring his enemies.
claims.note: The story is first told by Aeneas Sylvius Piccolomini, later Pope Pius II, in his history of Bohemia decades afterwards. No Czech source of the time mentions it.

claims.text: The radical Hussite armies were finally beaten by other Hussites.
claims.note: At Lipany the winning side was a league of Utraquist (moderate Hussite) and Catholic nobles and the Old Town of Prague. The battle is well recorded.

reigns.hook: Sigismund is king in Prague at last, aged 68. To see why the Czechs fought him so long, go back to the summer of 1419 and the dead king's younger brother.

reigns.tagline: The heir Bohemia fought off for seventeen years
reigns.cameToPower: Heir by blood, rejected by Hussites
reigns.reignEnded: Died at Znojmo, heading for Hungary
reigns.previously: The Hussite wars are over. Now rewind to 1419 and the heir they hated.
paragraphs: Sigismund was already King of Hungary and King of the Romans when his brother Wenceslaus died. He should have walked into Prague. Instead he was the most hated man in Bohemia. In 1414 he had given Jan Hus a safe conduct to the Council of Constance, then stood by while the council burned him. To most Czechs that was plain betrayal.

He came anyway, at the head of a crusade. On 28 July 1420, two weeks after his army was beaten at Vítkov, he had himself crowned in St Vitus Cathedral, inside the castle his men still held. On 1 November 1420 the Hussites routed him again below Vyšehrad. He left Bohemia and spent the next sixteen years trying to get back in, mostly with other people's armies.

In the end he got in by talking. He accepted the Compacts, which let the Czechs keep the communion cup, and entered Prague on 23 August 1436, by then a crowned emperor. He had just over a year. He began bringing Catholic priests back, and the old suspicion returned. In December 1437, sick and on his way to Hungary, he died at Znojmo in Moravia.

claims.text: Sigismund broke his word to Jan Hus.
claims.note: His safe conduct promised Hus safe travel. The council argued no promise could protect a heretic, and Sigismund went along with it. Czechs saw betrayal; his defenders saw a king trapped by the Church.

claims.text: Czechs nicknamed him “the red fox”.
claims.note: The name, for his reddish hair and slippery dealing, lives on in Czech tradition. It is hard to trace back to a source from his own lifetime.

claims.text: He was crowned King of Bohemia in 1420, while the Hussites held the city below.
claims.note: The coronation in St Vitus on 28 July 1420 is recorded by the Hussite chronicler Lawrence of Březová, among others.

reigns.hook: Sigismund dies with no son. He has picked his daughter's husband, Albert of Habsburg, to follow him. Half of Bohemia agrees. The other half sends for a Polish prince.

reigns.tagline: A Habsburg crown that lasted a year and a half
reigns.previously: Sigismund dies at Znojmo, leaving his crowns to his son-in-law.
paragraphs: Albert was Duke of Austria, a serious, steady man married to Sigismund's only daughter, Elizabeth. Within a few months he collected Hungary, Germany and Bohemia. In Bohemia the Catholic lords and many moderate Hussites accepted him, and he was crowned in Prague on 29 June 1438. The radicals had other ideas. They offered the crown to Casimir, the young brother of the King of Poland, and a Polish army came to back him.

Fighting dragged on around Tábor, and Albert never really settled Bohemia. Hungary needed him more, because the Ottoman Turks were pressing on its southern border. In 1439 he led an army down the Danube, caught dysentery in the camp and died on the way home in October. He left no son. His wife was pregnant, and everything now hung on whether the baby was a boy.

claims.text: The Hussite party chose a Polish prince, Casimir, as king against Albert.
claims.note: Recorded in Czech and Polish sources. Casimir, the future Casimir IV of Poland, was only a boy and never reigned in Bohemia.

claims.text: Albert made his dysentery worse by gorging on melons.
claims.note: A colourful detail repeated by chroniclers. There is no way to check it.

claims.text: He was the first Habsburg on the Bohemian throne since 1307.
claims.note: He is often called the first Habsburg king, but Albert I's son Rudolf briefly held the crown in 1306–07.

reigns.hook: Albert is dead. Four months later his widow gives birth to a boy, who is king from his first breath. Bohemia will wait a long time to see him.

reigns.tagline: Born a king, dead at seventeen
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Son of Albert II, born after his death
reigns.cameToPower: Born four months after his father died
reigns.previously: Albert dies of dysentery. His widow is pregnant.
paragraphs: Ladislaus arrived on 22 February 1440, a king from the day he was born. His mother had the Hungarian crown smuggled out of Visegrád castle so she could crown him as a baby. Bohemia was more careful. The lords agreed he was king, but nobody handed him over. The boy grew up at the court of his guardian, the German king Frederick III, while Bohemia ran itself through regional leagues of nobles and towns.

The strongman who emerged was George of Poděbrady, a Utraquist lord. In September 1448 his men seized Prague in a night raid, and in 1452 the diet made him land administrator. When the Austrians finally prised Ladislaus away from Frederick, George brought him to Prague, and on 28 October 1453 the boy was crowned in St Vitus. George went on running the country day to day.

In November 1457 Ladislaus was in Prague, planning his wedding to Madeleine, a daughter of the King of France. A grand French embassy was on its way. Then he fell ill and died within days, aged 17. People whispered poison, and fingers pointed at George, the man with most to gain. The king had no son and no brother. Bohemia had to find a king of its own.

claims.text: Ladislaus was poisoned, perhaps on George of Poděbrady's orders.
claims.note: Rumours spread at once. In the 1980s the anthropologist Emanuel Vlček examined his remains and concluded he most likely died of acute leukaemia.

claims.text: His mother's lady-in-waiting stole the Holy Crown of Hungary so the baby could be crowned.
claims.note: Helene Kottanner took it from Visegrád in 1440 and wrote her own account of the theft.

reigns.hook: The boy king is dead and there is no heir in sight. For the first time in centuries, the Czechs choose one of their own: George of Poděbrady, the man some say killed Ladislaus.

reigns.tagline: The Hussite king who wanted peace for all Europe
reigns.cameToPower: Elected by the diet in Prague
reigns.previously: Ladislaus dies suddenly at 17, just before his French wedding.
paragraphs: George was a Czech lord with no royal blood, and a Utraquist, one of the moderate Hussites who took communion from the cup. On 2 March 1458 the diet met in Prague's Old Town Hall and elected him king. To get crowned, he quietly swore obedience to the Pope, and two Hungarian bishops crowned him that May. He was a capable ruler, and for a few years Bohemia had peace and a king who spoke its language.

He also had big ideas. In 1464 his envoys toured Europe pitching a league of Christian princes, with a shared assembly to settle their quarrels and a joint front against the Turks. Rome had no time for a heretic king's plans. Pope Paul II excommunicated George and in 1466 declared him deposed. Catholic lords rose against him, and Matthias Corvinus of Hungary, once his son-in-law, invaded.

In 1469 George trapped Matthias's army at Vilémov and let him go on a promise of peace talks. Matthias went to Olomouc instead, where Catholic lords elected him King of Bohemia. George knew his own sons could not hold the crown against the Pope and Hungary together. So he passed them over and offered it to a Polish prince, Vladislaus. He died in Prague in March 1471.

claims.text: George's peace league was a forerunner of the European Union.
claims.note: The 1464 treaty draft is real and survives. Calling it the first plan for the EU is a modern framing, popular in Czech celebrations of him.

claims.text: He secretly swore obedience to Rome before his coronation.
claims.note: The oath was taken privately before the crowning bishops. George later said it did not touch the Compacts, which is what turned Rome against him.

reigns.hook: George is dead. The Polish prince he picked is fifteen, and Matthias Corvinus still claims to be King of Bohemia. Two kings, one crown.

reigns.previously: The pope calls a crusade against the Hussite king George.
paragraphs: The Catholic lords of Bohemia, backed by the pope, elected the Hungarian king Matthias Corvinus as their king against George of Poděbrady in 1469. He conquered Moravia, Silesia and Lusatia.
After George died, the Bohemians chose Vladislaus Jagiellon instead. The peace of Olomouc in 1479 let both men call themselves King of Bohemia, with Matthias keeping the outer lands until he died.
reigns.hook: Back in Prague, the Polish prince George picked is just fifteen. For nineteen years Bohemia will have two kings and one crown.
